newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - World wheat stocks set to stay tight. [CORRECTED 14:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - World wheat stocks set to stay tight. [CORRECTED 14:35 GMT]

text.p: Global wheat stocks look set to remain tight, new predictions from a leading international authority showed on Thursday.
(Corrects to delete reference to possible wheat shortages).
London-based experts the International Grains Council (IGC) forecast that an increase in wheat production would be soaked up by greater usage in 1997-98.
"The demand can be met because we have an increase in production," the IGC's Bill De Maria, told Reuters.
The IGC predicted a rise in world wheat output to 583 million tonnes this year, from 1996's 579.5 million tonnes.
But it also forecast world wheat usage to rise to 582 million tonnes from 556 million tonnes leaving little chance to rebuild stocks.
With governments ever less willing to hold wheat -- as seen in the now tiny size of the once notorious European Union "Grain Mountain" -- the onus is on a constant flow of supply.
"Production is all-important now that we don't have a large volume of carryover," De Maria said.
The IGC forecast carryover stocks to stay at 100 million tonnes, unchanged from 1996-97, and vastly reduced from previous years.

The crux of the problem stems from China where the IGC forecast an increase in imports to 7.0 million tonnes from 4.0 million previously, to be matched by a two million tonne increase in use, to 120 million tonnes.
Increased demand in Far East Asia and from a rapidly expanding population in India were also key to the forecast uptrend in consumption.
The IGC also saw increased wheat usage in the Former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as demand for animal feed recovers from a dip over several years amid the upheavals in the region.

Low reserves make trade an essential element in smoothing out the ups and downs of supply and demand, De Maria said. And the IGC pointed out that, if Russia and China are ignored, world wheat trade remains on a steady up-trend.
